title: Fuga ex Troia. Creusa amissa
titleEn: The Flight from Troy and the Loss of Creusa — Aeneid II.689–804
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Aeneas, telling Dido of Troy's last night, has watched his father Anchises refuse to leave the burning city. Now the old man lifts his hands and prays to Jupiter: if prayers can move him, let him look on them and, if they deserve it, confirm the omen. Hardly has he spoken when thunder rolls on the left and a star falls through the dark, trailing a torch of light over the roof and into the woods of Ida, leaving a furrow of sulphurous smoke behind it. Anchises is overcome; he rises, salutes the gods and the holy star, and agrees to follow. The fire is growing louder, and Aeneas gives his orders: his father is to ride on his shoulders, little Iulus is to walk at his side, and Creusa is to follow at a distance; all are to meet at an old mound and a deserted shrine of Ceres outside the city, where stands an ancient cypress. Anchises is to carry the sacred objects and the household gods, since Aeneas, fresh from the slaughter, may not touch them until he has washed in running water. He puts a cloak and a lion's skin over his shoulders and takes up his father; Iulus clings to his hand, and Creusa comes behind. The man who was unmoved by spears is now frightened by every breeze. Near the gates a sound of tramping feet seems to come close, and Anchises cries out that he sees shields and bronze gleaming. Then some unfriendly power takes away Aeneas' wits, and in his flight along unknown byways Creusa is lost: whether she stopped, strayed or sat down exhausted he never learns. He does not look back until they reach Ceres' mound, and there she alone is missing. He lodges his son, his father and the Penates with his companions in a hidden valley, puts on his armour again and goes back through the streets to look for her, retracing his steps, finding their house already taken by the Greeks and in flames, and Priam's palace, where Phoenix and Ulysses guard the heaped-up plunder and the captives. He calls her name in the empty streets, until her phantom, taller than in life, appears before his eyes. She tells him not to grieve: it is by the gods' will that she cannot go with him. He is to sail a long exile to the land of Hesperia, where the Tiber flows, and there a kingdom and a royal wife await him; she herself will not be a slave to Greek women, for the Great Mother keeps her on these shores. She bids him farewell and to love their son, and fades. Three times he tries to embrace her, and three times the image slips from his hands like a breeze or a dream. At dawn he goes back to find a great crowd of new followers gathered, ready for exile, with the Greeks holding the gates and no hope of help. Aeneas gives way, lifts his father and makes for the mountains.
part: The Flight from Troy and the Loss of Creusa (II.689–804)

sentences.t:
“Iuppiter omnipotens, precibus si flecteris ullis,
aspice nos;
sentences.l:
“Jupiter almighty, if by any prayers you are bent,
look on us;
sentences.i: “Almighty Jupiter, if any prayers can move you, look upon us;
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and the beginning of Anchises' prayer, with the opening “. He has lifted his hands to heaven (688). 'flecteris' is the second person singular present passive (the ending -ris for -re) of 'flecto', 'you are bent, swayed'; 'precibus… ullis' is an ablative of means. 'aspice' is the imperative of 'aspicio'; the object is 'nos'.

sentences.t:
hoc tantum, et, si pietate meremur,
da deinde auxilium, pater, atque haec omina firma.”
sentences.l:
this only, and, if by piety we deserve,
give then help, father, and these omens firm.”
sentences.i: this only I ask; and if our devotion earns it, then grant us help, Father, and make these omens sure.”
sentences.n: 'hoc tantum' has its verb of asking left out, 'this only (I ask)': an ellipsis. 'pietate' is an ablative of cause. 'meremur' is the first person plural of the deponent 'mereor', here used without an object, 'we deserve (it)'. 'da' is the imperative of 'do'; 'pater' is a vocative, Jupiter; 'haec omina firma' is 'these omens (grant) firm', that is, 'confirm them'. The closing ” ends the prayer.

sentences.t:
Vix ea fatus erat senior, subitoque fragore
intonuit laevum, et de caelo lapsa per umbras
stella facem ducens multa cum luce cucurrit.
sentences.l:
Scarcely these things had spoken the old man, and with sudden crash
it thundered on the left, and from the sky gliding through the shadows
a star leading a torch with much light ran.
sentences.i: Scarcely had the old man spoken when, with a sudden crash, it thundered on the left, and a star slid down from the sky through the darkness, drawing a fiery trail and racing along in a great blaze of light.
sentences.n: 'Vix ea fatus erat' is the pluperfect of the deponent 'for', 'fari' (the perfect participle 'fatus' with 'erat'), 'had spoken'; 'senior' is the comparative of 'senex' used as a noun, 'the elder man', Anchises. 'subito… fragore' is an ablative of manner. 'laevum' is a neuter accusative used as an adverb, 'on the left'; for Roman augurs, thunder on the left was a favourable sign. 'intonuit' is the perfect of 'intono' (used impersonally, 'it thundered'). 'lapsa' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'labor', 'gliding, having slipped'. 'facem' is the object of 'ducens', 'drawing a torch', the star's trail. 'cum' stands between 'multa' and 'luce', 'with much light'.

sentences.i: We watched it glide over the topmost gables of the house and bury itself, shining, in the woods of Ida, marking out the road as it went;
sentences.n: 'cernimus' takes an accusative and infinitive, 'we see her (the star) hide herself': 'illam… condere'. 'labentem' is the present participle of 'labor' and 'illam' is the star ('stella', feminine). 'summa super… culmina' has 'super' placed between the adjective and its noun; 'culmina tecti' are the ridges of the roof. 'claram' is predicative, 'bright'. 'Idaea… silva' is an ablative of place without a preposition (ordinary in verse); Ida is the mountain behind Troy. 'signantem vias' means 'marking out its ways': the star leaves a mark of light across the sky as it goes.

sentences.t:
tum longo limite sulcus
dat lucem, et late circum loca sulphure fumant.
sentences.l:
then in a long track the furrow
gives light, and widely around the places with sulphur smoke.
sentences.i: then a furrow of light lies along a lengthy track, and far around the country smokes with sulphur.
sentences.n: 'longo limite' is an ablative of the way along which, or of manner, 'along a long track'; 'sulcus' (a furrow, as the plough makes) is the trail of the star. 'dat lucem' is 'gives light'. 'loca' is a neuter plural, 'places, the country'; 'circum' is an adverb, 'round about'; 'sulphure' is an ablative of means. The unit begins in the middle of line 697, after the semicolon.

sentences.t:
Hic vero victus genitor se tollit ad auras,
adfaturque deos et sanctum sidus adorat.
sentences.l:
Here indeed conquered the father himself raises to the breezes,
and addresses the gods and the holy star adores.
sentences.i: Then indeed my father, won over, lifts himself up into the open air, speaks to the gods, and worships the sacred star.
sentences.n: 'Hic vero' is 'at this point indeed'. 'victus' is the perfect passive participle of 'vinco', 'overcome': his refusal to leave (638–649) now yields. 'genitor' is Anchises. 'se tollit ad auras' is 'raises himself to the air', that is, stands upright. 'adfaturque' is 'adfatur' (the present of the deponent 'adfor', Greenough's spelling) with '-que'. 'adorat' is 'worships'; the present tenses are the vivid narrative present.

sentences.t: “Iam iam nulla mora est; sequor et qua ducitis adsum.
sentences.l: “Now, now no delay there is; I follow and where you lead I am present.
sentences.i: “No more delay now, no more; I follow, and I am here wherever you lead.
sentences.n: Anchises' speech begins with “. 'iam iam' is a doubled adverb for urgency, 'now, now at last'. 'nulla mora est' is 'there is no delay'. 'qua' is a relative adverb, 'by whatever way, where'; 'ducitis' is addressed to the gods; 'adsum' is 'I am at hand, I am there'.

sentences.t: Di patrii, servate domum, servate nepotem.
sentences.l: Gods of our fathers, preserve the house, preserve the grandson.
sentences.i: Gods of our fathers, keep our house safe; keep my grandson safe.
sentences.n: 'Di' is the vocative plural of 'deus' in its contracted form, and 'patrii' is 'of the fatherland, ancestral': these are the ancestral gods of the house (the Penates are named separately at 717). 'servate' is an imperative, repeated (anaphora). 'domum' is the household, the family line; 'nepotem' is the grandson Iulus.

sentences.t: Vestrum hoc augurium, vestroque in numine Troia est.
sentences.l: Yours this augury, and in your divinity Troy is.
sentences.i: This omen is yours, and Troy stands within your power.
sentences.n: 'Vestrum' is the neuter possessive adjective agreeing with 'augurium', 'yours' ('est' understood); it is not the genitive plural of 'vos'. 'vestro… in numine' is 'in your divine power or will'; 'Troia est' is 'Troy exists, Troy stands': its survival lies with the gods.

sentences.t: Cedo equidem, nec, nate, tibi comes ire recuso.”
sentences.l: I yield indeed, nor, son, to you a companion to go do I refuse.”
sentences.i: I yield; and I do not refuse, my son, to go with you as your companion.”
sentences.n: 'cedo' is 'I yield, give way'; 'equidem' is 'for my part, indeed'. 'nec… recuso' takes the infinitive 'ire', 'I do not refuse to go'. 'nate' is a vocative; 'tibi comes' is 'as a companion to you', with 'comes' a predicate nominative. The closing ” ends the speech.

sentences.t: Dixerat ille;
sentences.l: He had spoken;
sentences.i: So he had spoken;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Dixerat' is the pluperfect of 'dico', 'had spoken', with 'ille' (Anchises) as subject. Greenough's semicolon runs the sentence on into the sound of the fire.

sentences.t:
et iam per moenia clarior ignis
auditur, propiusque aestus incendia volvunt.
sentences.l:
and now through the walls clearer the fire
is heard, and nearer the heat the conflagrations roll.
sentences.i: and now the fire is heard more plainly through the city walls, and the blazes roll their surges of heat nearer.
sentences.n: 'clarior' is the comparative of 'clarus', here of sound, 'more clearly'; 'ignis' is the nominative singular and 'auditur' the present passive, 'is heard'. 'propius' is the comparative adverb, 'nearer'. 'incendia' is the subject (the conflagrations) and 'aestus' the accusative plural of the fourth-declension noun 'aestus', 'heat, surges of heat', object of 'volvunt'. The unit begins in the middle of line 705.

sentences.t: “Ergo age, care pater, cervici imponere nostrae;
sentences.l: “Therefore come, dear father, on my neck be set;
sentences.i: “Come then, dear father, settle yourself upon my neck;
sentences.n: Aeneas' speech begins here with “. 'Ergo age' is 'well then, come'. 'imponere' is the second person singular imperative of the passive (middle) 'imponor', 'place yourself, be set'; 'cervici nostrae' is a dative with the compound verb, and 'nostrae' is simply 'mine'.

sentences.t: ipse subibo umeris, nec me labor iste gravabit:
sentences.l: I myself shall go under with shoulders, nor me that toil shall burden:
sentences.i: I shall go beneath you myself, with my shoulders, and that labour will not weigh me down:
sentences.n: 'subibo' is the future of 'subeo', 'go under, take the load'; 'umeris' is an ablative of means. 'iste' is 'that (of yours)', the burden he is about to carry. 'gravabit' is the future of 'gravo', 'weigh down'. The colon introduces the reason.

sentences.t:
quo res cumque cadent, unum et commune periclum,
una salus ambobus erit.
sentences.l:
wherever things whatsoever shall fall, one and common the danger,
one the safety for both shall be.
sentences.i: Wherever things may fall, the danger will be one and shared, and there will be one safety for us both.
sentences.n: 'quo res cumque cadent' is 'quocumque' split in two, a tmesis ('wherever things shall fall out'); the verb is a future indicative, as often in a general clause of this kind. 'periclum' is Greenough's spelling of 'periculum' (the syncopated form; you'll see this constantly). 'unum et commune' and 'una' repeat the one idea; 'ambobus' is a dative of advantage, 'for both of us'. The unit ends in the middle of line 710.

sentences.t:
Mihi parvus Iulus
sit comes, et longe servet vestigia coniunx:
sentences.l:
To me little Iulus
let be companion, and at a distance let keep the footsteps my wife:
sentences.i: Let little Iulus be my companion, and let my wife follow in my steps at a distance:
sentences.n: 'sit' and 'servet' are jussive subjunctives (A&G: a command in the third person). 'mihi… comes' is 'a companion to me'. 'servet vestigia' is 'keep to the footsteps, follow behind'. 'coniunx' is Creusa, told to follow at a distance. In 'coniunx' the i is a consonant, 'con-iunx'. The unit begins in the middle of line 710.

sentences.t: vos, famuli, quae dicam, animis advertite vestris.
sentences.l: you, servants, what I shall say, to your minds turn.
sentences.i: You, servants, take to heart what I am about to say.
sentences.n: 'famuli' is a vocative, the household servants. 'quae dicam' is a relative clause, 'what I am going to say'; 'dicam' is first person singular, either future or present subjunctive. 'animis… advertite' is 'turn (your attention) with your minds', the usual 'animum advertere' with the object left to be understood; 'animis' is an ablative of means.

sentences.t:
Est urbe egressis tumulus templumque vetustum
desertae Cereris, iuxtaque antiqua cupressus
religione patrum multos servata per annos.
sentences.l:
There is, for those having gone out from the city, a mound and a temple ancient
of deserted Ceres, and beside it an old cypress
by the religion of our fathers preserved through many years.
sentences.i: Outside the city, as you go out, there is a mound, and the ancient temple of forsaken Ceres, and beside it an old cypress, kept safe through many years by our fathers' reverence.
sentences.n: 'Est' opens the sentence, 'there is'. 'urbe egressis' is a dative plural of the perfect participle of the deponent 'egredior', 'for those who have gone out', with the ablative of separation 'urbe'. 'templum… Cereris' is the temple of Ceres, 'desertae' being 'abandoned'. 'iuxta' is an adverb, 'close by'. 'cupressus' is a feminine noun (tree names), so 'antiqua' and 'servata' agree with it. 'religione patrum' is an ablative of cause, 'by the reverence of our fathers'.

sentences.t: Hanc ex diverso sedem veniemus in unam.
sentences.l: This from different directions place we shall come into one.
sentences.i: By different ways we shall all come to this one place.
sentences.n: 'hanc… sedem' is an accusative of goal, 'to this place', and 'in unam' repeats it, 'into one (place)': the two words frame the line. 'ex diverso' is 'from different directions', an adjective used as a noun. 'veniemus' is the future of 'venio'.

sentences.t: Tu, genitor, cape sacra manu patriosque Penatis;
sentences.l: You, father, take the sacred things in your hand and the ancestral Penates;
sentences.i: You, Father, take the holy things in your hand, and the household gods of our fathers;
sentences.n: 'sacra' is a neuter plural, 'sacred objects', the cult objects of the family; 'manu' is an ablative of means. 'Penatis' is an accusative plural in -is (you'll see this constantly). The Penates are Troy's household gods; carrying them to Italy is part of Aeneas' task (see I.6 'inferretque deos Latio').

sentences.t:
me, bello e tanto digressum et caede recenti,
attrectare nefas, donec me flumine vivo
abluero.”
sentences.l:
me, from war so great having departed and from slaughter recent,
to handle is impious, until me in a stream living
I shall have washed.”
sentences.i: for me, fresh from such a war and from newly shed blood, it is a sin to touch them until I have washed myself in running water.”
sentences.n: 'me… attrectare nefas' is an accusative and infinitive with 'nefas' (est) as the predicate, 'for me to handle them is a sin'. 'digressum' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'digredior', 'having come away', agreeing with 'me'. 'bello e tanto… et caede recenti' are both ablatives of separation. 'donec… abluero' is a future perfect, 'until I shall have washed', and 'flumine vivo' is 'in running water'. Blood-guilt required ritual washing before sacred things were touched. Line 720, 'abluero', is a half-line: Greenough prints it as a short line of its own, one of Virgil's unfinished verses. The closing ” ends the speech.

sentences.i: With these words I spread a cloak over my broad shoulders and bowed neck, and above it the skin of a tawny lion, and bend beneath the load;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Haec fatus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'for', 'having said' (active in sense; you'll see this constantly). 'insternor' is a passive in a middle sense, 'I cover myself', followed by the accusatives of respect 'latos umeros subiectaque colla' (a Greek construction): 'covered in respect of my shoulders and neck'. 'subiecta' is 'bent down, put beneath' the burden. 'veste super' has 'super' as an adverb, 'a cloak over (it)'; 'fulvi… pelle leonis' is an ablative of means. 'succedo oneri' is 'I go under the load', 'succedo' taking the dative.

sentences.t:
dextrae se parvus Iulus
implicuit sequiturque patrem non passibus aequis;
sentences.l:
to my right hand himself little Iulus
has entwined and follows his father not with equal steps;
sentences.i: little Iulus has twined himself about my right hand, and follows his father with steps unequal to his;
sentences.n: 'dextrae' is a dative with 'implicuit', 'has entwined himself in (my) right hand'; 'se' is the object. 'implicuit' (perfect) and 'sequitur' (present) stand side by side, as the tenses often do in this narrative. 'non passibus aequis' is an ablative of manner, 'with unequal steps': the child's short stride against his father's. The unit begins in the middle of line 723.

sentences.t: pone subit coniunx: ferimur per opaca locorum;
sentences.l: behind comes up my wife: we are borne through the dark of places;
sentences.i: behind us comes my wife; we make our way through shadowy places;
sentences.n: 'pone' is an adverb, 'behind'. 'subit' is 'comes up, follows'. 'opaca locorum' is a neuter plural adjective with a partitive genitive (A&G: 'the shady parts of the places'). 'ferimur' is the passive of 'fero', 'we are carried', that is, 'we make our way'.

sentences.t:
et me, quem dudum non ulla iniecta movebant
tela neque adverso glomerati ex agmine Grai,
nunc omnes terrent aurae, sonus excitat omnis
suspensum et pariter comitique onerique timentem.
sentences.l:
and me, whom a little while ago not any hurled
weapons moved, nor from the opposing line massed Greeks,
now all the breezes terrify, every sound alarms
anxious and equally for companion and for burden fearing.
sentences.i: And I, whom a while ago no flying spear could move, nor the Greeks massed in the line against me, am frightened now by every breeze, and every sound startles me, hanging in suspense and equally afraid for my companion and my burden.
sentences.n: 'me' is the object of 'terrent' and 'excitat' and the antecedent of 'quem'; the relative clause comes first. 'dudum' is 'a short while ago'. 'iniecta… tela' is 'weapons thrown at (me)'. 'adverso… ex agmine' is 'from the line facing me', and 'glomerati' (the perfect participle of 'glomero') 'massed together'; 'Grai' is the contracted nominative plural of 'Graius' ('Graii'). Greenough prints 'ex agmine', the Latin Library 'examine' ('from the swarm'): the sense is almost the same. 'omnis' in 'sonus excitat omnis' is the nominative singular, 'every sound'. 'suspensum' is 'in suspense, on the stretch'. 'comiti onerique' are datives with 'timentem': 'fearing for' takes the dative of the person for whom.

sentences.t:
Iamque propinquabam portis, omnemque videbar
evasisse viam, subito cum creber ad auris
visus adesse pedum sonitus, genitorque per umbram
prospiciens;
sentences.l:
And now I was drawing near the gates, and the whole
way I seemed to have got through, when suddenly thick to the ears
seemed to be present the sound of feet, and my father through the shadow
looking ahead;
sentences.i: I was by now close to the gates and thought I had come safely through the whole road, when suddenly the thick tramp of feet seemed to be at our ears, and my father, peering ahead through the gloom;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'videbar' is the passive 'I seemed', with the infinitive 'evasisse' (the perfect infinitive of 'evado', 'to have got through'): a personal construction, 'I seemed to have escaped'. 'omnem… viam' is the object. 'cum… visus (est)' is the inverse 'cum' with the perfect, in which the new event comes in the 'cum' clause; 'visus… adesse' is 'seemed to be present'. 'creber' agrees with 'sonitus' (held apart from it, with 'ad auris' between), 'thick, coming close together'. 'ad auris' is an accusative plural in -is. 'prospiciens' is the participle of 'genitor', whose verb 'exclamat' comes in the next unit.

sentences.t: “Nate exclamat, fuge nate, propinquant.”
sentences.l: “Son, he cries, flee, son, they are approaching.”
sentences.i: “Son,” he cries, “flee, my son; they are drawing near.”
sentences.n: Anchises' cry begins mid-line with Greenough's “. 'exclamat' is a verb of speaking set inside the speech (cf. 'ait' at 639); the subject 'genitor' is in the preceding unit. 'nate… nate' is a vocative repeated for urgency; 'fuge' is an imperative. 'propinquant' is 'they are drawing near' (the Greeks, unstated).

sentences.t: “Ardentis clipeos atque aera micantia cerno!”—
sentences.l: “Blazing shields and bronze flashing I see!”—
sentences.i: “I see their blazing shields and the flash of their bronze!”—
sentences.n: Anchises' cry goes on, in a second pair of quotation marks as Greenough prints it. 'ardentis' is an accusative plural in -is, 'blazing' (with the glitter of firelight). 'aera' is a neuter plural, 'bronze (weapons and armour)', with 'micantia', 'flashing'. The dash follows the closing ”: the narrative breaks off the scene and plunges into the loss of Creusa; the unit ends at the dash.

sentences.t:
Hic mihi nescio quod trepido male numen amicum
confusam eripuit mentem.
sentences.l:
Here to me, trembling, some I-know-not-what ill-friendly
power snatched my confused mind.
sentences.i: Then some power, I could not tell which, no friend to me, took my shaken wits from me in my terror.
sentences.n: 'nescio quod' is a fixed expression, 'some… or other' (A&G: 'nescio quis' acts as an indefinite). 'numen' is a neuter noun, 'divine power', unnamed; 'male amicum' is 'ill-disposed, unfriendly' ('male' turns the adjective toward its opposite). 'mihi… trepido' is a dative of disadvantage with 'eripuit', 'snatched from me, trembling'. 'confusam… mentem' is 'my confused mind'. 'eripuit' is the perfect of 'eripio'. The reason follows.

sentences.t:
Namque avia cursu
dum sequor, et nota excedo regione viarum,
heu, misero coniunx fatone erepta Creüsa
substitit, erravitne via, seu lassa resedit,
incertum;
sentences.i: For while I ran on, following byways and leaving the familiar quarter of the streets, whether my wife Creusa, taken from wretched me by fate, stopped, or strayed from the road, or sat down worn out, is not known;
sentences.n: 'avia' is a neuter plural, 'pathless places', the object of 'sequor'; 'cursu' is an ablative of manner. 'dum sequor' is 'while I follow', the present tense with 'dum' in a past narrative. 'nota excedo regione viarum' is 'I leave the known region of the streets': 'excedo' with an ablative of separation, 'nota' agreeing with 'regione'. 'heu' is an interjection of grief. 'misero' is a dative of disadvantage with 'erepta', 'taken from wretched (me)'. 'fatone… erravitne… seu… resedit' is a triple indirect question (the enclitic '-ne' 'whether', then 'seu' 'or whether') depending on 'incertum (est)', 'it is uncertain': the three questions are the subject. 'substitit' is the perfect of 'subsisto', 'halted, stood still'. 'lassa' is 'weary'; the Latin Library reads 'lapsa' ('slipped, fallen'), which changes the sense a little. 'Creüsa' has a diaeresis, three syllables, Cre-ü-sa. The unit begins in the middle of line 736.

sentences.t: nec post oculis est reddita nostris.
sentences.l: nor afterwards to eyes was she restored ours.
sentences.i: nor was she ever afterwards given back to our sight.
sentences.n: 'est reddita' is the perfect passive of 'reddo', 'was restored', 'nec' standing before 'post' ('and not afterwards'). 'oculis nostris' is a dative of the person to whom. Aeneas states the loss with understatement.

sentences.i: I did not look back for her, lost as she was, or turn my thoughts to her, until we reached the mound of ancient Ceres and the hallowed place;
sentences.n: 'prius… quam' are split apart ('priusquam'), 'not before… than', with the perfect indicative 'venimus' (the event actually happened). 'amissam' is the perfect participle of 'amitto', 'lost', agreeing with the 'her' understood as object of 'respexi'. 'respexi' is the perfect of 'respicio', 'look back', and 'animum reflexi' 'turned my mind back'. 'sedem sacratam' is 'the consecrated seat', the shrine. The place is the meeting-point of 713–715.

sentences.t:
hic demum collectis omnibus una
defuit, et comites natumque virumque fefellit.
sentences.l:
here at last, all having been gathered, she alone
was missing, and companions and son and husband she deceived.
sentences.i: There at last, when all were gathered, she alone was missing, and had slipped away unnoticed from her companions, her son and her husband.
sentences.n: 'hic demum' is 'here at last'. 'collectis omnibus' is an ablative absolute. 'una' is a nominative, 'she alone', agreeing with the subject (Creusa, unnamed). 'defuit' is the perfect of 'desum'. 'fefellit' is the perfect of 'fallo', 'deceived, escaped the notice of', and takes the accusatives 'comites… natumque virumque'; the double '-que' pairs son and husband. The unit begins in the middle of line 743.

sentences.t:
Quem non incusavi amens hominumque deorumque,
aut quid in eversa vidi crudelius urbe?
sentences.l:
Whom not did I accuse, frantic, of men and of gods,
or what in the overturned city did I see more cruel?
sentences.i: Whom, in my frenzy, did I not blame, of men or of gods? Or what crueller thing did I see in the overthrown city?
sentences.n: 'Quem… hominumque deorumque' is 'whom of men and of gods', a partitive genitive depending on 'quem'; the double '-que' makes 'both men and gods'. 'Quem… non incusavi' is a rhetorical question ('whom did I not blame?') whose answer is 'everyone'. 'amens' is a nominative, 'out of my mind'. 'quid… crudelius' is the neuter interrogative with a comparative, 'what (thing) crueller?', and 'vidi' is the perfect; 'eversa… urbe' is 'the overturned city'.

sentences.t:
Ascanium Anchisenque patrem Teucrosque Penatis
commendo sociis et curva valle recondo;
sentences.l:
Ascanius and Anchises the father and the Teucrian Penates
I commit to companions and in a curved valley hide;
sentences.i: I entrust Ascanius, my father Anchises, and the Trojan household gods to my companions, and hide them in a winding valley;
sentences.n: 'Anchisen' is a Greek accusative in -en (you'll see this constantly with names), with 'patrem' in apposition. 'Teucros' is an adjective agreeing with 'Penatis' ('Trojan household gods'): 'Teucri', the Trojans, are named for the early king Teucer; 'Penatis' is an accusative plural in -is. 'commendo' is 'I entrust', and 'recondo' 'I put away, hide'; both are in the present, which here carries the narrative forward. 'curva valle' is an ablative of place.

sentences.t: ipse urbem repeto et cingor fulgentibus armis.
sentences.l: I myself the city go back to and am girded with gleaming arms.
sentences.i: I go back to the city myself and put on my shining armour.
sentences.n: 'repeto' is 'I seek again, go back to'. 'cingor' is a passive with a middle sense, 'I gird myself' (A&G); 'fulgentibus armis' is an ablative of means, the participle of 'fulgeo' meaning 'gleaming'.

sentences.t:
Stat casus renovare omnis, omnemque reverti
per Troiam, et rursus caput obiectare periclis.
sentences.l:
It stands to renew all chances, and the whole to go back
through Troy, and again my head to expose to dangers.
sentences.i: I am resolved to risk every hazard again, to go back through all of Troy, and once more to put my head in the way of danger.
sentences.n: 'Stat' is impersonal, 'it is fixed, it stands resolved', with three infinitives: 'renovare', 'reverti' (the present infinitive of the deponent 'revertor') and 'obiectare'. 'casus omnis' is an accusative plural in -is, 'all the chances, all the hazards'; 'renovare' is 'to renew' them. 'omnem… per Troiam' frames the phrase, 'the whole of Troy'. 'caput' is 'my head', that is, my life; 'obiectare' is 'to expose', a frequentative of 'obicio'. 'periclis' is a dative, Greenough's syncopated spelling of 'periculis'.

sentences.t:
Principio muros obscuraque limina portae,
qua gressum extuleram, repeto, et vestigia retro
observata sequor per noctem et lumine lustro.
sentences.l:
First the walls and the dark threshold of the gate,
where my step I had brought out, I seek again, and my footprints back
observed I follow through the night and with light I scan.
sentences.i: First I return to the walls and the dark threshold of the gate by which I had come out, and follow my own tracks, marked as I went, back through the night, scanning them with my eyes.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'principio' is an ablative used as an adverb, 'at the start'. 'muros… limina portae' are the objects of 'repeto'. 'qua' is a relative adverb, 'by which'; 'gressum extuleram' is the pluperfect, 'I had carried out my step', that is, 'gone out'. 'vestigia… observata' is the perfect participle, 'noted, kept in view'; 'retro' is an adverb with 'sequor'. 'lumine lustro': 'lumen' in verse can mean 'the eye', so 'I survey with my eyes'; 'lustro' is 'I scan'.

sentences.t: Horror ubique animo, simul ipsa silentia terrent.
sentences.l: Horror everywhere to my mind, at once the very silences terrify.
sentences.i: Dread is everywhere in my mind, and the very silence adds to the terror.
sentences.n: 'Horror ubique animo' has 'est' left out; 'animo' is a dative of reference or an ablative of place, 'in my mind'. 'simul' is 'at the same time'. 'silentia' is a poetic plural, 'the silences'; 'ipsa' 'the very'.

sentences.t:
Inde domum, si forte pedem, si forte tulisset,
me refero:
sentences.l:
Then home, if by chance the foot, if by chance she had borne it,
I bring myself back:
sentences.i: Then I carry myself home, in case — in case — she had turned her steps there:
sentences.n: 'si forte' is 'if by chance, in case', used of a hoped-for event, and is repeated for emphasis. 'tulisset' is the pluperfect subjunctive of 'fero'; 'pedem… tulisset' is 'had carried her foot', 'had gone', with Creusa understood as subject. 'me refero' is 'I carry myself back, I return'. The colon introduces what he found.

sentences.t: inruerant Danai, et tectum omne tenebant.
sentences.l: had rushed in the Danaans, and the building entire they were holding.
sentences.i: The Greeks had burst in and held the whole house.
sentences.n: 'inruerant' is the pluperfect of 'inruo' (Greenough's spelling, for 'irruo'), 'had rushed in'. 'Danai' is the nominative plural, 'the Greeks'. 'tectum omne' is 'the whole roof', that is, 'the whole house'; 'tenebant' is the imperfect, 'were holding'. The unit begins in the middle of line 757.

sentences.t:
Ilicet ignis edax summa ad fastigia vento
volvitur;
sentences.l:
At once the fire devouring to the highest gables by the wind
is rolled;
sentences.i: At once the devouring fire is rolled by the wind up to the topmost gables;
sentences.n: 'Ilicet' is 'at once, forthwith' (from 'ire licet', 'you may go', the formula for dismissing a meeting). 'ignis edax' is 'devouring fire'. 'summa ad fastigia' has the preposition between adjective and noun. 'vento' is an ablative of means; 'volvitur' is a passive with a middle sense, 'rolls itself, is rolled'.

sentences.t: exsuperant flammae, furit aestus ad auras.
sentences.l: rise up, the flames; rages the heat to the air.
sentences.i: the flames mount higher, and the heat rages up to the sky.
sentences.n: 'exsuperant' is 'rise above, surmount', used here without an object ('flammae' is its subject). 'aestus' is a nominative singular of the fourth declension, 'heat, surge'; 'ad auras' is 'to the air, the sky'. The unit begins in the middle of line 759.

sentences.t: Procedo et Priami sedes arcemque reviso.
sentences.l: I advance and Priam's seat and the citadel revisit.
sentences.i: I go on and revisit Priam's palace and the citadel.
sentences.n: 'sedes' is an accusative plural, 'dwelling, palace'; 'Priami sedes arcemque' are the objects of 'reviso', 'I go back to see'.

sentences.t:
Et iam porticibus vacuis Iunonis asylo
custodes lecti Phoenix et dirus Ulixes
praedam adservabant.
sentences.l:
And now in the empty colonnades, in Juno's sanctuary,
guards chosen, Phoenix and dread Ulysses,
the plunder were guarding.
sentences.i: And already, in the empty colonnades, in Juno's sanctuary, picked guards, Phoenix and fearsome Ulysses, were watching over the spoil.
sentences.n: 'porticibus vacuis' is an ablative of place, and 'Iunonis asylo' is an ablative in apposition, 'in Juno's sanctuary' ('asylum' is a Greek word for a place of refuge, and here the precinct of Juno's temple). 'custodes lecti' is 'chosen guards'. 'Phoenix' is a Greek captain here, presumably Achilles' old tutor from the Iliad, not a Phoenician. 'dirus Ulixes' is 'dread Ulysses' ('Ulixes' is the Latin form of Odysseus). 'adservabant' is the imperfect, Greenough's spelling of 'asservabant', 'were guarding'.

sentences.t:
Huc undique Troia gaza
incensis erepta adytis, mensaeque deorum,
crateresque auro solidi, captivaque vestis
congeritur;
sentences.i: Hither from every side the treasure of Troy, torn from the burning shrines, is heaped up: the tables of the gods, bowls of solid gold, and captured garments;
sentences.n: 'Troia gaza' is 'Trojan treasure' ('gaza' is a loan word of Persian origin); 'Troia' is an adjective. 'incensis… adytis' is an ablative of separation, 'from the burned inner shrines'. 'mensae deorum' are the tables where offerings were set out for the gods. 'crateres' is a nominative plural, the large mixing-bowls, and 'auro solidi' is 'solid in gold', that is, of solid gold. 'captiva… vestis' is 'captured raiment', 'vestis' being a collective singular. 'congeritur' is singular because it agrees with the nearest subject, 'vestis'; the verb has the whole list as subject.

sentences.t:
pueri et pavidae longo ordine matres
stant circum.
sentences.l:
boys and fearful mothers in a long line
stand around.
sentences.i: boys and frightened mothers stand around in a long line.
sentences.n: 'pueri et pavidae… matres' are the captives guarded with the plunder. 'longo ordine' is an ablative of manner, 'in a long row', and 'circum' is an adverb, 'round about'. Line 767, 'stant circum', is a half-line: Greenough prints it as a short line of its own, one of Virgil's unfinished verses. The unit begins in the middle of line 766.

sentences.t:
Ausus quin etiam voces iactare per umbram
implevi clamore vias, maestusque Creüsam
nequiquam ingeminans iterumque iterumque vocavi.
sentences.l:
Having dared, indeed even, voices to cast through the shadow
I filled with shouting the ways, and sorrowful Creusa
in vain redoubling again and again I called.
sentences.i: I even dared to fling my voice out through the darkness, and filled the streets with my shouting; and sorrowing, in vain, I called Creusa again and again, over and over.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Ausus' is the perfect participle of the semi-deponent 'audeo', 'having dared' (active in sense), and takes the infinitive 'iactare', 'to fling out'. 'quin etiam' is 'nay, even', adding a further point. 'implevi… clamore vias' is 'I filled the streets with shouting' ('clamore' ablative of means). 'maestus' is a nominative agreeing with the speaker; 'nequiquam' is 'in vain'; 'ingeminans' is the present participle of 'ingemino', 'redoubling (the cry)'. 'iterumque iterumque' is 'again and again'.

sentences.t:
Quaerenti et tectis urbis sine fine furenti
infelix simulacrum atque ipsius umbra Creüsae
visa mihi ante oculos et nota maior imago.
sentences.l:
To me seeking and through the roofs of the city without end raging
unhappy a phantom and of Creusa herself the shade
appeared to me before my eyes and, than known, greater, an image.
sentences.i: As I searched and raged without end through the buildings of the city, there appeared before my eyes the sorrowful phantom, the very shade of Creusa, an image larger than the one I knew.
sentences.n: 'Quaerenti… furenti' are datives of the present participles, agreeing with 'mihi' ('visa mihi'), 'to me searching and raging'. 'tectis urbis' is 'through the houses of the city', an ablative of place. 'sine fine' is 'without end'. 'infelix simulacrum atque… umbra… imago' are three names for one apparition; 'visa' is the perfect passive participle with 'est' left out, 'was seen, appeared', agreeing with the nearest subject, 'imago'. 'nota maior' is 'greater than the known (form)', 'nota' an ablative of comparison: so she looks larger than the Creusa he knew. The Latin Library reads 'ruenti' ('rushing') for Greenough's 'furenti' ('raging'), a small difference of sense.

sentences.t: Obstipui, steteruntque comae et vox faucibus haesit.
sentences.l: I was stunned, and stood up my hair and my voice in my throat stuck.
sentences.i: I was struck dumb; the hair rose on my head, and my voice clung to my throat.
sentences.n: 'obstipui' is the perfect of 'obstipesco', 'I was stupefied'. 'steteruntque' is 'steterunt' (the perfect of 'sto' with the -erunt ending, 'stood on end') with '-que'; 'comae' is the nominative plural, 'hair'. 'faucibus' is an ablative of place, 'in the throat', and 'haesit' the perfect of 'haereo'. The line is a formula for terror that the poet uses again elsewhere in the poem.

sentences.t: [Tum sic adfari et curas his demere dictis :]
sentences.l: [Then thus to address and cares with these words to take away:]
sentences.i: [Then she began to speak, and to take my cares away with such words:]
sentences.n: Greenough prints this line in square brackets as spurious (an addition to the text); we keep it. The two infinitives 'adfari' (the deponent infinitive of 'adfor') and 'demere' have no verb on which to depend, and could only be read as historical infinitives, 'then she (spoke)…', an awkward construction that may be why the line is bracketed. 'curas… demere' is 'to remove (my) cares', and 'his… dictis' is an ablative of means. The ghost's speech follows.

sentences.t:
“Quid tantum insano iuvat indulgere dolori,
O dulcis coniunx?
sentences.l:
“What so much to a mad grief does it please to indulge,
O sweet husband?
sentences.i: “Why does it please you to give yourself so far to this senseless grief, my sweet husband?
sentences.n: Creusa's speech begins, with the opening “. 'quid' is an accusative of respect used as an adverb, 'why?'. 'iuvat' is impersonal, 'it pleases', followed by the infinitive 'indulgere', which takes the dative 'insano dolori'. 'tantum' is an adverb, 'so much, so far'. 'coniunx' is here masculine, 'husband' (the word is common in gender); 'O dulcis coniunx' is a vocative.

sentences.t:
Non haec sine numine divom
eveniunt;
sentences.l:
Not these things without the divine will of the gods
happen;
sentences.i: These things do not come about without the will of the gods;
sentences.n: 'divom' is the old genitive plural in -om (you'll see this constantly). 'sine numine' is 'without the divine will'. 'eveniunt' is the present of 'evenio', 'come to pass'. The unit begins in the middle of line 777.

sentences.t:
nec te hinc comitem asportare Creüsam
fas, aut ille sinit superi regnator Olympi.
sentences.l:
nor you from here as companion to carry Creusa
is right, or he allows, the ruler of high Olympus.
sentences.i: nor is it right for you to take Creusa hence as your companion, nor will he allow it, the ruler of high Olympus.
sentences.n: 'te… asportare… fas' is an accusative and infinitive with 'fas (est)' under the 'nec': 'it is not right that you carry off'. 'comitem' is predicative, 'as a companion', and 'Creüsam' is the object of 'asportare'. The Latin Library prints the line a little differently ('portare Creusam' for 'asportare Creüsam', with 'comitem' placed elsewhere): the sense is the same. 'hinc' is 'from here'. 'ille… superi regnator Olympi' is Jupiter, 'that ruler of high Olympus' ('superi' is the genitive of 'superus', 'upper').

sentences.t:
Longa tibi exsilia, et vastum maris aequor arandum,
et terram Hesperiam venies, ubi Lydius arva
inter opima virum leni fluit agmine Thybris:
sentences.l:
Long for you exiles, and the vast of the sea expanse to be ploughed,
and to the land Hesperian you will come, where the Lydian among fields
rich of men with gentle flow flows Tiber:
sentences.i: Long exile is yours, and a vast plain of sea to plough; and you will come to the land of Hesperia, where the Lydian Tiber flows with gentle current among fields rich in men:
sentences.n: 'Longa tibi exsilia' leaves out 'sunt': 'for you (are) long exiles', with 'tibi' a dative. 'vastum maris aequor arandum' is a gerundive of obligation, 'the wide plain of the sea (is) to be ploughed': the metaphor of ploughing the sea. 'terram Hesperiam venies' has an accusative of goal without a preposition, 'Hesperia' being the 'western land', Italy. 'Lydius… Thybris' is the Tiber, 'Lydian' because the Etruscans who lived along it were said to have come from Lydia; 'Thybris' is the Greek form of the name. 'arva inter opima virum' has 'inter' after its noun, with 'virum' for 'virorum' (the old genitive plural, you'll see this constantly), 'fields rich in men'; 'leni… agmine' is an ablative of manner. The colon introduces the promise.

sentences.t:
illic res laetae regnumque et regia coniunx
parta tibi.
sentences.l:
there prosperous affairs and a kingdom and a royal wife
won for you.
sentences.i: there prosperity, and a kingdom, and a royal wife are won for you.
sentences.n: 'illic' is 'there'. 'res laetae' are 'happy fortunes'. 'regia coniunx' is a royal wife, Lavinia, daughter of Latinus; she is not named. 'parta' is the perfect passive participle of 'pario', 'obtained, secured', neuter plural agreeing with the mixed list, with 'sunt' left out; 'tibi' is a dative of advantage. The unit ends in the middle of line 784.

sentences.t: Lacrimas dilectae pelle Creüsae.
sentences.l: Tears for beloved Creusa drive away.
sentences.i: Drive away your tears for your beloved Creusa.
sentences.n: 'Lacrimas… dilectae… Creüsae' is 'tears for beloved Creusa', 'Creüsae' being an objective genitive; she speaks of herself in the third person. 'pelle' is the imperative of 'pello', 'drive away'. 'dilectae' is the perfect participle of 'diligo', 'beloved'.

sentences.t:
Non ego Myrmidonum sedes Dolopumve superbas
aspiciam, aut Graiis servitum matribus ibo,
Dardanis, et divae Veneris nurus.
sentences.l:
Not I the Myrmidons' abodes or of the Dolopes the proud
shall look upon, or to Greek matrons to be a slave shall go,
a Dardan woman, and of divine Venus daughter-in-law.
sentences.i: I shall never look upon the proud homes of the Myrmidons or the Dolopes, or go to serve Greek matrons, I, a Dardan woman, and the daughter-in-law of the goddess Venus.
sentences.n: 'Myrmidonum' and 'Dolopum' are genitive plurals in -um (Greek-style names): the Myrmidons and Dolopes are peoples of Thessaly, Achilles' home country, where a Trojan captive might be taken. '-ve' is 'or'; 'sedes' is an accusative plural and 'superbas' 'proud'. 'aspiciam' is the future of 'aspicio'. 'servitum ibo' has a supine in -um after a verb of motion, expressing purpose, 'I shall go to serve', and 'matribus' is a dative with 'servio'. 'Graiis' is the poetic adjective 'Graius' (for 'Graecus'), 'Greek', dative plural agreeing with 'matribus' (the Latin Library's 'Grais' is the same word, contracted). 'Dardanis' is a nominative, 'a Dardan woman', in apposition to the speaker, and 'nurus' is a nominative singular, 'daughter-in-law': Creusa is the wife of Venus' son. Line 787, 'Dardanis, et divae Veneris nurus', is a half-line: Greenough prints it as a short line of its own, one of Virgil's unfinished verses.

sentences.t: Sed me magna deum genetrix his detinet oris:
sentences.l: But me the great of the gods mother on these shores detains:
sentences.i: But the great Mother of the gods keeps me here on these shores:
sentences.n: 'deum' is the genitive plural in -um contracted for 'deorum'. 'magna deum genetrix' is Cybele, the Great Mother, whose cult belonged to Mount Ida and the Trojan region; she keeps Creusa on these shores of Troy, and Virgil says no more of how. 'his… oris' is an ablative of place, 'on these shores', and 'detinet' 'holds back'.

sentences.t: iamque vale, et nati serva communis amorem.”
sentences.l: and now farewell, and of the son common keep the love.”
sentences.i: And now farewell, and keep your love for the son we share.”
sentences.n: 'iamque vale' is 'and now farewell' ('vale' is the imperative of 'valeo', 'be well'). 'nati communis amorem' is 'love of our common son' ('nati communis' a genitive, objective with 'amorem'); 'serva' is an imperative, 'keep'. The closing ” ends Creusa's speech.

sentences.t:
Haec ubi dicta dedit, lacrimantem et multa volentem
dicere deseruit, tenuisque recessit in auras.
sentences.l:
These sayings when she had given, weeping and many things wishing
to say she left, and thin she withdrew into the air.
sentences.i: When she had said this, she left me weeping and wanting to say much more, and, growing thin, faded into the air.
sentences.n: 'Haec ubi dicta dedit' is 'when she had given these sayings', the periphrasis for 'when she had spoken'; 'dicta' is the object and 'dedit' the perfect of 'do'. 'lacrimantem et multa volentem dicere' are accusative present participles agreeing with 'me' (unstated, the object of 'deseruit'); 'multa' is the neuter plural object of 'dicere'. 'tenuis' is a nominative singular feminine, 'thin, insubstantial', agreeing with the ghost; 'recessit in auras' is 'withdrew into the air'.

sentences.t: Ter conatus ibi collo dare bracchia circum:
sentences.l: Thrice I tried there to her neck to give arms around:
sentences.i: Three times I tried, there, to throw my arms around her neck:
sentences.n: 'conatus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'conor', used as a finite verb with 'sum' left out, 'I tried'. 'collo dare bracchia circum' is a tmesis ('circumdare') with 'collo' a dative, 'to put the arms around her neck'. 'bracchia' is Greenough's spelling. The colon introduces the three failures. The scene echoes Odysseus' meeting with his mother's shade in the underworld (Odyssey, Book 11), where he tries three times to embrace her and she slips away.

sentences.t:
ter frustra comprensa manus effugit imago,
par levibus ventis volucrique simillima somno.
sentences.l:
thrice in vain grasped from the hands escaped the image,
equal to light winds and most like to a winged sleep.
sentences.i: three times the image, grasped in vain, slipped from my hands, as light as the breezes and most like a sleep that flies.
sentences.n: 'ter' is repeated from the previous line. 'comprensa' is the perfect participle of 'comprehendo' agreeing with 'imago', 'grasped'. 'manus' is an accusative plural, the object of 'effugit' ('escaped my hands'). 'par levibus ventis' is 'equal to light winds', 'par' taking the dative; 'simillima' is a superlative with the dative 'somno', 'most like to sleep'. 'volucri somno' is 'winged, fleeting sleep'. These lines recur at VI.700–702, where Aeneas tries to embrace the shade of Anchises (there Greenough spells 'brachia' and prints the third line, 'par levibus ventis…', in square brackets).

sentences.t: Sic demum socios consumpta nocte reviso.
sentences.l: Thus at last companions, the night spent, I revisit.
sentences.i: So at length, with the night used up, I go back to my companions.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Sic demum' is 'thus at last'. 'consumpta nocte' is an ablative absolute, 'the night being used up'. 'reviso' is the present of 'reviso', 'go back to see', repeating 'reviso' of 760.

sentences.t:
Atque hic ingentem comitum adfluxisse novorum
invenio admirans numerum, matresque virosque,
collectam exsilio pubem, miserabile volgus.
sentences.l:
And here a huge of companions to have flowed in new
I find, wondering, number, both mothers and men,
a youth gathered for exile, a pitiable crowd.
sentences.i: And here, to my wonder, I find that a vast number of new companions has flowed in, mothers and men, a band gathered for exile, a pitiable throng.
sentences.n: 'invenio' takes an accusative and infinitive: 'ingentem comitum… novorum… numerum' is the subject accusative of 'adfluxisse', the perfect infinitive of 'adfluo', 'to have flowed in'; 'admirans' is a present participle, 'wondering'. 'matresque virosque' is a double '-que', 'both mothers and men', in apposition to 'numerum'. 'collectam exsilio pubem' is 'a youth (the grown people) gathered for exile', 'exsilio' being a dative of purpose. 'volgus' is Greenough's spelling of 'vulgus' (the Latin Library prints 'uulgus'); it is neuter, so 'miserabile' agrees with it.

sentences.t:
Undique convenere, animis opibusque parati,
in quascumque velim pelago deducere terras.
sentences.l:
From all sides they had come together, in spirit and in resources prepared,
to whatever I might wish by sea to lead lands.
sentences.i: From every side they had gathered, ready in spirit and in means, for whatever lands I might choose to lead them to over the sea.
sentences.n: 'convenere' is 'convenerunt' (-ere for -erunt; you'll see this constantly). 'animis opibusque' are ablatives of respect, 'in spirit and in resources'; 'parati' is a predicate, 'ready'. 'in quascumque velim… terras' has 'cumque' attached to 'quas' (the relative 'quascumque'); 'velim' is a present subjunctive, 'I might wish' (the clause says what they stand ready for), and 'deducere' is the infinitive completing it, 'to lead (them) down (to the sea)'. 'pelago' is an ablative of means or route, 'over the sea'.

sentences.i: And now Lucifer was rising over the ridges of high Ida and bringing on the day; the Greeks held the beleaguered gates, and no hope of help was offered;
sentences.n: 'iugis' is an ablative of place, 'on the ridges', and 'summae Idae' a genitive. 'Lucifer' is the morning star ('light-bringer'). 'ducebat diem' is 'was leading on the day'. 'obsessa' is the perfect passive participle of 'obsideo', 'besieged, beset', agreeing with 'limina'; 'tenebant' is the imperfect, 'were holding'. 'nec spes opis ulla dabatur' is 'and no hope of help was being given'. The imperfects set the scene for the decision.

sentences.t: cessi, et sublato montes genitore petivi.
sentences.l: I yielded, and having lifted my father the mountains I sought.
sentences.i: I gave way, and, lifting up my father, made for the mountains.
sentences.n: 'cessi' is the perfect of 'cedo', 'I yielded, gave way', the verb Anchises used of himself at 704. 'sublato… genitore' is an ablative absolute, 'my father having been lifted up' ('sublato' from 'tollo'). 'montes' is an accusative plural, Greenough's reading (the Latin Library has 'montis', the same case in another spelling). 'petivi' is the perfect of 'peto'. This is the last line of Book II.
